metadata.title: Examining the relationship between online chatting and PISA reading literacy trends (2000-2018)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA microdata to compute country-level aggregates and then models country-level trend changes. For each PISA year, student-level sampling weights (W_FSTUWT) are used to compute unbiased national averages/percentages (e.g., reading literacy means, internet-at-home percentages, and other reading-related indicators). Because the analysis ultimately treats countries as the units of analysis, the authors further construct country weights based on the total number of students represented by each country’s national samples, averaged across the available PISA waves, and then standardize these weights so the average across countries equals 1 to avoid miscalculation of statistical significance. Replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are not reported; instead, the weighting strategy is implemented through country-level weights in the multilevel and path-analytic steps.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the main analyses are country-level trend-change estimates derived from multilevel modeling of PISA reading literacy averages and from country-level changes in self-reported behaviors (online chatting, reading fiction, and reading strategies). The paper does not describe plausible-value (PV) generation/combination or a PV-based achievement modeling workflow, because the analysis is conducted on aggregated reading literacy trend-change parameters rather than on student-level PV outcomes. Missing data handling is also not specified at the PV level; the authors instead report that there were no missing data at the country level for the trend-change variables used.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses PISA reading literacy waves from 2000–2018 but restricts the country set to those that participated in the first PISA survey (2000/2002), with explicit exclusions: Liechtenstein is excluded after its participation ended (only until 2012), the Netherlands is excluded for not meeting PISA sample requirements, and two countries from PISA 2000 plus one from PISA 2002 are excluded. The study includes all available reading literacy measurements for each included country from 2000 through 2018 (up to seven measurements per country), while online chatting and reading fiction are available only in subsets of waves (chatting: 2009 and 2018; fiction: 2000/2002, 2009, 2018). Reading strategies are only available for 2009 and 2018, so only the 2009–2018 change is analyzed for that construct. The main unit of analysis is country-level trend-change estimates derived from multilevel modeling; the paper reports no missing data at the country level for the trend-change variables used.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000–2018 Reading literacy (15-year-olds), country-level trend changes (2000/2002, 2009, 2018)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-level correlations: Online chatting ↔ Reading literacy r = −0.698 (p < 0.001). Path model (lavaan): standardized paths Online chatting → Reading literacy β = −0.378 (p = 0.009); Reading fiction → Reading literacy β = 0.219 (p = 0.005); Reading strategies → Reading literacy β = 0.386 (p = 0.007). Model explains 64.1% of variance in reading literacy trend changes; fit: χ² p = 0.998; TLI ≈ 1.000; RMSEA/SRMR reported as favorable (exact values not provided in excerpt).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000–2018 reading literacy data aggregated to country-level trend changes, the study leveraged online chatting trend change, reading fiction trend change, and reading strategies awareness change to predict reading literacy trend change, finding that faster online chatting growth after 2009 coincided with decelerating reading literacy trends (β = −0.378, p = 0.009), while increases in reading fiction and reading strategies were positively associated with reading literacy trend changes. This indicates that education policy should prioritize sustaining and promoting reading fiction and explicit instruction/assessment of effective reading strategies as part of responses to rapidly changing out-of-school digital communication environments, while noting that the design is correlational and not causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes country-level trend changes in PISA reading literacy for 15-year-olds across 39 countries over 2000–2018, focusing on shifts after 2009 (the period following the iPhone and WhatsApp). Reading literacy trend changes are estimated via multilevel modeling with cross-sectional repeated measures, and then related to country-level trend changes in online chatting prevalence (available for 2009 and 2018), reading fiction prevalence (2000/2002, 2009, 2018), and awareness of useful reading strategies (change only for 2009–2018). The strongest bivariate association is between online chatting and reading literacy (r = −0.698, p < 0.001). In the path model estimated with lavaan, online chatting has a negative direct association with reading literacy trend change (β = −0.378, p = 0.009), while reading fiction and reading strategies show positive associations (β = 0.219, p = 0.005; β = 0.386, p = 0.007). The model accounts for 64.1% of variance, but the approach is correlational (no causal identification) and uses country-level aggregates rather than student-level PV-based prediction.
